reading.title: The slow return of the night train
reading.text:
For three decades the sleeper train looked like a relic. Between 1990 and 2015 most European operators withdrew their overnight services, and the reasoning was straightforward: budget airlines had made short flights extraordinarily cheap, while sleeper carriages were expensive to maintain and could only be sold once a night. A seat on a daytime train can be sold four or five times in a day; a bunk cannot.

Since 2016, however, the picture has changed. Austria's national operator, which had quietly bought up rolling stock that other companies were discarding, expanded its network year after year and reported that the routes were profitable. Other operators followed, and by 2022 several new lines had opened between major capitals. Commentators frequently attribute this revival to environmental awareness, and it is true that a night train produces a small fraction of the emissions of an equivalent flight. Yet operators themselves tend to give a more prosaic explanation. Passengers, they say, are buying a hotel room that moves, and the calculation only works when the fare is compared with a flight plus a night's accommodation plus two airport transfers.

The obstacles that remain are largely administrative rather than technical. A train crossing four countries must satisfy four sets of safety rules, four signalling systems and, in some cases, four separate ticketing platforms. Track access charges are levied by each national infrastructure manager, and because these charges are calculated per kilometre regardless of the hour, a slow overnight service pays the same as a fast daytime one for occupying the line. Reformers argue that until this pricing is revised, the revival will remain confined to a handful of politically favoured routes.

reading.title: Why bridges are over-designed
reading.text:
Ask a structural engineer how much load a bridge can carry and the honest answer is: considerably more than it will ever be asked to. Codes of practice typically require a structure to withstand between one and a half and two times the heaviest load it is expected to encounter. This margin is known as the factor of safety, and the phrase is slightly misleading, because the factor is not a measure of ignorance about the loads. Traffic weights are, in fact, well understood. The margin exists because the materials themselves vary.

A batch of concrete poured on a cold Tuesday will not have precisely the strength of a batch poured the following week; a steel section may contain a flaw invisible from the surface. Engineers therefore design not to the average strength of a material but to a characteristic value, conventionally the strength that ninety-five per cent of samples will exceed. The safety factor is then applied on top of that already conservative figure.

Critics of the approach point out that it is expensive. Excess material means excess cost and, increasingly relevant, excess embodied carbon, since cement production alone accounts for a substantial share of global emissions. A movement within the profession now argues for what it calls proportionate design: applying the full margin where failure would be catastrophic and sudden, and a reduced one where a structure would give visible warning before collapsing. The distinction matters. A steel beam sags conspicuously long before it fails, whereas certain concrete columns fail without warning at all.

The counter-argument is not really technical. It is that structures outlive the assumptions made about them. A footbridge designed in 1975 for pedestrians may today carry service vehicles, and no code can anticipate how a building will be used in eighty years. The margin, on this view, is not waste but an inheritance left to future users.

reading.title: The economics of the coffee cup
reading.text:
A cup of coffee bought in a European city costs perhaps three euros. Of that sum, the grower receives somewhere between three and nine cents. The figure is regularly quoted to illustrate exploitation, and the imbalance is real, but the arithmetic is more complicated than the headline suggests. Most of the price paid by the customer covers costs incurred in the country where the cup is sold: rent on a city-centre site, wages, equipment, energy and tax. Roasting, packaging and shipping absorb a further share.

What the figure does capture accurately is where value is added, and where it is not. Green coffee — the unroasted bean — is a commodity, traded on exchanges and largely interchangeable. Roasted, branded coffee is not. The step from commodity to branded product is where margins expand, and that step almost always takes place outside the country of origin. Producing nations have long recognised this and have periodically attempted to roast and export finished coffee themselves. Few have succeeded at scale. The obstacles include tariff structures that historically taxed processed goods more heavily than raw ones, the short shelf life of roasted beans, and the difficulty of building a consumer brand in a distant market.

Certification schemes offer a partial response by guaranteeing a minimum price, though their effect is debated. A guaranteed floor protects growers when prices collapse, but critics note that it may also encourage production of ordinary coffee when the greater gain lies in quality. The specialty market, which pays several times the commodity rate for distinctive lots, has grown quickly, and some cooperatives have prospered within it. That route, however, demands consistent quality, traceability and direct relationships with buyers — capacities that are themselves expensive to build.

reading.title: Reading the rings
reading.text:
Dendrochronology — the dating of events by tree rings — began as a byproduct of astronomy. In the early twentieth century an American astronomer studying sunspot cycles suspected that solar activity might leave a trace in the growth of trees, and started measuring ring widths in the pines of the south-western United States. The sunspot hypothesis proved inconclusive, but the method he developed to compare samples turned out to be extraordinarily powerful.

The principle is cross-dating. Because trees in a region respond to the same droughts and cold summers, the pattern of wide and narrow rings is shared, functioning rather like a barcode. A living tree provides a sequence anchored to the present; a beam from an old building overlaps that sequence at its outer end and extends it backwards; timber from an archaeological site overlaps the beam in turn. Chained together, such sequences now reach back more than eight thousand years in parts of Europe.

The technique has an unusual property among dating methods: within its range it produces a calendar year, not an estimate with error bars. This precision has repeatedly embarrassed other lines of evidence. Buildings confidently dated on stylistic grounds have been shown to be decades younger than assumed, and radiocarbon dating itself is now calibrated against tree-ring sequences rather than the reverse.

Its limitations are equally distinctive. It works only where trees experience a marked growing season, so tropical species with no clear annual rings are largely unusable. It requires enough rings — a short sequence of thirty or forty may match several positions by chance. And it dates the felling of the tree, not the construction of whatever was built from it. Timber was often stockpiled, reused, or transported considerable distances, so a precise felling date is the beginning of an argument about a building, not the end of one.

reading.title: Learning to sleep badly
reading.text:
Insomnia is usually described as a failure to sleep, but clinicians who treat it often describe it instead as a learned association. A person has a difficult few nights for an ordinary reason — illness, a deadline, a noisy neighbour — and begins to worry about sleeping. The worry is then rehearsed in the bedroom, night after night, until the room itself becomes a cue for alertness rather than rest. What began as a temporary disturbance has been trained into a habit.

This account explains why the most effective treatment is behavioural rather than pharmacological. Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia works by breaking the association. Patients are told to leave the bedroom if they have not fallen asleep within about twenty minutes, and to return only when sleepy. They are also given a restricted window in bed, often considerably shorter than the time they currently spend there. The restriction is uncomfortable at first and reliably unpopular, but it concentrates sleep and rebuilds the link between bed and sleeping.

Trials consistently find that the effects outlast those of medication. Sleeping tablets work quickly and are effective in the short term, but their benefit fades when they are stopped, whereas behavioural gains are typically maintained a year later. Despite this, prescribing remains far more common than referral to therapy in most health systems, largely because therapy requires trained practitioners and several weekly sessions, while a prescription takes two minutes.

There is also a measurement problem that complicates the field. People with insomnia routinely underestimate how long they have slept, sometimes by two hours or more, and a proportion of those who report severe insomnia sleep normally according to laboratory recording. Whether this represents a distinct condition or an extreme of ordinary misperception remains disputed.

reading.title: The map that was mostly guesswork
reading.text:
Early modern maps are often admired for their beauty and mistrusted for their accuracy, and the second judgement deserves qualification. A sixteenth-century chart of the Atlantic coast could be remarkably precise about the details that mattered to its users — the depth of an anchorage, the bearing between two headlands — while being wildly wrong about the interior of a continent a hundred kilometres inland. The map was not a general description of the world. It was an instrument for a particular task, and its accuracy was distributed accordingly.

This explains a feature that puzzles modern viewers: the confident depiction of places nobody had visited. Blank space on a chart was commercially awkward, since a purchaser wanted a complete document, and cartographers filled gaps by combining sailors' reports, classical authority and inference from coastlines. The resulting features were not always understood as speculation by those who copied them. A river drawn tentatively in one decade could appear as an established fact in the next, and might survive for a century after expeditions had failed to find it.

Historians of cartography have therefore become cautious about treating maps as records of knowledge. They are better read as records of what was believed, wanted or claimed. A boundary drawn firmly through unsurveyed territory may tell us nothing about the ground and a great deal about a political claim being asserted. Some of the most informative maps, on this reading, are the least accurate ones, because the errors are not random. They cluster where interests were strongest.

reading.title: Rewilding and its critics
reading.text:
Rewilding proposes that the most effective conservation is often the least managed. Instead of maintaining a habitat in a fixed condition — mowing a meadow, coppicing a wood — the approach removes intervention, reinstates large herbivores or predators where possible, and allows the system to find its own arrangement. Proponents point to sites where species richness rose sharply within a decade after intensive management stopped.

The strongest evidence comes from grazing. Large herbivores create structural variety: they trample, browse unevenly, open gaps and leave dung that supports invertebrates. A landscape shaped by animals is patchy in ways that mechanical management rarely reproduces. In several European projects, free-roaming cattle and ponies substituting for extinct wild grazers have produced habitat mosaics that scarce birds and insects have colonised quickly.

Critics raise two objections that are not easily dismissed. The first is that many valued habitats in Europe are themselves the product of centuries of human management, and abandoning that management does not restore an original condition but creates a new one, often dominated by scrub. Species adapted to the older regime may be lost in the process. The second concerns land. Rewilding at meaningful scale requires large continuous areas, and in densely settled countries these are typically farmland, so the debate becomes one about food production and rural employment rather than ecology.

Supporters answer that the choice is rarely all or nothing, and that marginal land — steep, wet or unproductive — could be released without materially affecting output. That argument has gained traction, though it also concedes something important: on the best land, conventional conservation is likely to remain the only realistic option.

reading.title: The problem of the average
reading.text:
In the 1940s the United States Air Force investigated an unusually high rate of accidents among its pilots. Having eliminated training and mechanical failure, investigators turned to the cockpit itself, which had been dimensioned in 1926 using the average measurements of several hundred pilots. A researcher was asked to check whether the averages had drifted upwards. He measured over four thousand pilots on ten dimensions and then asked a question nobody had thought to ask: how many of them were close to average on all ten? The answer was none. Even on three dimensions, fewer than one in twenty qualified.

The conclusion was not that the averages were wrong but that designing for the average produced an object that fitted nobody. The response — adjustable seats, pedals and straps — is now so familiar that its novelty is hard to recall, and accident rates fell.

The episode is frequently retold as a lesson about ergonomics, but its deeper implication concerns statistics. An average is a summary of a distribution, not a description of a member of it, and the two are easily confused when the average is treated as a type. The confusion recurs wherever a single figure is used to stand for a varied population: a typical patient's response to a drug, a representative student's progress, an ordinary household's energy use. In each case the average may be a perfectly accurate summary while describing nobody in particular.

What the cockpit case adds is a practical corrective. Where variation is large, the useful design question is not what the typical user needs but what range must be accommodated — and, crucially, whether the object can be made adjustable rather than fixed. That reframing costs something. Adjustability is more expensive to manufacture and more complicated to use, which is why the argument still has to be made repeatedly in fields that have not yet had their own cockpit moment.

reading.title: The quiet economics of repair
reading.text:
For most of the twentieth century, repair was ordinary. A radio, a kettle or a pair of shoes was expected to be mended several times before it was discarded, and most high streets supported at least one workshop that did nothing else. The decline of that trade is usually blamed on cheap manufacturing, and the price data appear to support the story: between 1970 and 2010 the real cost of most household electrical goods fell by more than eighty per cent, while the hourly cost of skilled labour rose steadily. Once an hour of a technician's time cost more than a replacement appliance, the economic argument for repair collapsed.

Yet price alone does not explain the whole shift. Design changed too, and it changed in ways that were rarely announced. Screws gave way to clips and then to adhesive; modular circuit boards gave way to sealed assemblies; batteries stopped being user-replaceable. Manufacturers describe these decisions in the language of slimness, waterproofing and reliability, and in fairness those benefits are real. But the same decisions have the side effect of transferring repair from the owner to the manufacturer, and often of removing it altogether.

The response, gathering pace since around 2015, has been a set of so-called right-to-repair campaigns. Their central demand is not that products should be built to last for ever, which no campaigner seriously proposes, but that spare parts, diagnostic software and service manuals should be available to independent workshops on the same terms as to authorised dealers. Several jurisdictions have now legislated in this direction. Early evidence from France, which introduced a repairability index in 2021, suggests that the score influences purchasing more than regulators expected, though it remains difficult to separate that effect from the general rise in environmental awareness over the same period.

reading.title: Memory as reconstruction
reading.text:
The intuition that memory works like a recording is remarkably persistent, and it is wrong in an interesting way. What the brain stores is not a copy of an event but a sparse set of traces — a gist, a few vivid details, an emotional tone — which are reassembled at the moment of recall. Reassembly is not neutral. It draws on general knowledge to fill gaps, and it is influenced by everything the rememberer has learned, said or been asked since.

This is why leading questions are so effective. In a classic series of experiments, participants who were asked how fast cars were going when they 'smashed into' each other later reported broken glass at a scene where there was none; those asked about cars that 'contacted' each other did not. The wording did not distort a stored image; it supplied material that the reconstruction then incorporated.

The practical consequences are uncomfortable, particularly in legal settings, where confidence is routinely treated as a proxy for accuracy. It is not a reliable one. Confidence measured immediately after an identification, and before any feedback, does carry real information. Confidence expressed months later in a courtroom, after the witness has been interviewed repeatedly and told that a suspect was charged, carries far less — and yet it is the courtroom figure that juries hear.

listening.title: Seminar: measuring poverty
listening.script: Absolute measures set a fixed threshold — an income sufficient for a defined basket of goods. Relative measures set the line as a proportion of median income, typically sixty per cent. The two behave very differently in a recession. If everyone's income falls together, absolute poverty rises, but relative poverty may actually fall, because the median has fallen too. That is not a paradox; it simply reflects that the measures answer different questions. Absolute measures ask whether people can meet basic needs. Relative measures ask whether they can participate normally in the society they live in.

listening.title: Lecture: why forecasts fail

Consider hurricane track prediction, which has improved dramatically, and hurricane intensity prediction, which has barely improved at all — using the same data. The difference lies in the physics. Track is governed by large-scale steering flows that models resolve well. Intensity depends on processes inside the eyewall at scales far below the grid resolution. More observations do not help if the model cannot represent the mechanism. The lesson generalises: before demanding more data, ask whether the limiting factor is measurement or understanding.

The chart shows the percentage of households with internet access in one European country between 2000 and 2020.

2000: 18% · 2005: 46% · 2010: 71% · 2015: 86% · 2020: 94%

Sleeping — Japan 6.8h, Spain 8.1h, Brazil 7.6h
Working — Japan 8.9h, Spain 6.4h, Brazil 7.2h
Commuting — Japan 1.4h, Spain 0.7h, Brazil 1.9h
Leisure — Japan 2.1h, Spain 4.3h, Brazil 3.0h

The diagram shows the process of producing bottled drinking water.

Groundwater extraction → sediment filtration → carbon filtration → UV sterilisation → bottling → labelling → distribution

The bar chart shows electricity generation by source in one country in 2005 and 2020.

2005 — coal 52%, gas 26%, nuclear 14%, renewables 8%
2020 — coal 12%, gas 31%, nuclear 15%, renewables 42%

The pie charts show household expenditure in one country in 1990 and 2020.

1990 — housing 24%, food 29%, transport 14%, leisure 9%, other 24%
2020 — housing 34%, food 17%, transport 15%, leisure 14%, other 20%

University A: 1,200 → 2,400 → 3,900
University B: 2,800 → 2,600 → 2,100
University C: 900 → 1,800 → 4,600

The table shows recycling rates in five cities in 2010 and 2022.

City 1: 22% → 58% · City 2: 41% → 49% · City 3: 15% → 63% · City 4: 55% → 57% · City 5: 8% → 31%

The diagram shows the life cycle of a domestic solar panel from manufacture to disposal.

Silicon refining → cell production → panel assembly → installation → 25 years of operation → decommissioning → glass and metal recovery → residual waste

The maps show a coastal town in 1985 and today.

1985 — small harbour, one hotel, farmland to the north, single coastal road
Today — expanded marina, four hotels, housing estate on former farmland, bypass road, pedestrianised seafront

The bar chart shows average monthly rainfall in three cities.

City X — Jan 15mm, Apr 40mm, Jul 190mm, Oct 60mm
City Y — Jan 85mm, Apr 70mm, Jul 25mm, Oct 90mm
City Z — Jan 45mm, Apr 48mm, Jul 51mm, Oct 46mm

1960 — agriculture 42%, industry 34%, services 24%
1990 — agriculture 18%, industry 32%, services 50%
2020 — agriculture 5%, industry 21%, services 74%

Food — A 100, B 132, C 74, D 118
Housing — A 100, B 165, C 52, D 141
Transport — A 100, B 121, C 89, D 96
Healthcare — A 100, B 88, C 61, D 173

The diagram shows how rainwater is harvested and used in a domestic building.

Roof collection → gutter and first-flush diverter → storage tank → filtration → pump → toilet flushing and garden irrigation; overflow to soakaway

The graph shows tourist arrivals and tourism revenue in one country from 2012 to 2022.

Arrivals (millions): 2.1 → 3.8 → 4.9 → 0.4 → 3.1
Revenue (US$ bn): 1.8 → 3.6 → 5.4 → 0.3 → 4.0
